questions.stem: Which of the following shows metals in the correct order of reactivity from most to least reactive?

options.text: Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, zinc
Gold, copper, iron, sodium, potassium
Iron, zinc, magnesium, sodium, potassium
Copper, iron, zinc, calcium, sodium

questions.explanation: The correct order from most to least reactive is: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold. Option B correctly lists the first five in this order.

questions.stem: What makes a metal more reactive?

options.text: It gains electrons more easily
It is harder and more dense
It loses electrons more easily to form positive ions
It has a higher melting point

questions.explanation: A more reactive metal loses its outer shell electrons more easily to form positive ions. This is why metals at the top of the reactivity series (like potassium and sodium) react vigorously, as they easily lose their outer electron.

questions.stem: Where does carbon sit in the reactivity series?

options.text: Below copper
Carbon is not placed in the reactivity series
Above potassium
Between aluminium and zinc

questions.explanation: Carbon is placed between aluminium and zinc in the reactivity series. This is important because carbon can be used to extract metals that are less reactive than itself (below it) by reduction, but not metals above it.

questions.stem: How was the reactivity series determined?

options.text: By observing the vigour of reactions of metals with water and acids
By measuring the density of each metal
By measuring the melting point of each metal
By observing the colour of each metal

questions.explanation: The reactivity series was established by observing how vigorously metals react with water, steam, and dilute acids. More reactive metals react more vigorously, producing gas more quickly and generating more heat.

questions.stem: Which pair of metals are found naturally in their pure (native) form because they are so unreactive?

options.text: Iron and zinc
Aluminium and magnesium
Potassium and sodium
Gold and platinum

questions.explanation: Gold and platinum are so unreactive that they are found naturally as pure metals (native). They do not easily combine with other elements. Very reactive metals like potassium and sodium are always found combined with other elements in compounds.

questions.stem: If a metal reacts vigorously with cold water, where in the reactivity series is it likely to be?

options.text: Near the top, with very reactive metals
It cannot be determined from this information
In the middle, with moderately reactive metals
Near the bottom, with unreactive metals

questions.explanation: Metals that react vigorously with cold water are very reactive and are found near the top of the reactivity series, such as potassium, sodium, and calcium. Less reactive metals only react with steam or dilute acids, or not at all.

questions.stem: Why is aluminium sometimes less reactive than expected despite being high in the reactivity series?

options.text: Because it forms a protective oxide layer on its surface
Because it is a non-metal
Because it has a very high melting point
Because it is a very light metal

questions.explanation: Aluminium forms a thin but tough layer of aluminium oxide on its surface when exposed to air. This oxide layer protects the metal underneath from further reaction, making aluminium appear less reactive than its position in the reactivity series suggests.
